claim: Genomic sequencing has implicated large numbers of genes and de novo mutations as potential disease risk factors.
source: Genomic sequencing has implicated large numbers of genes and de novo mutations as potential disease risk factors.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of genomic sequencing research, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: 134 genes were tested in the Drosophila heart using RNAi-based gene silencing.
source: 134 genes were tested in the Drosophila heart using RNAi-based gene silencing.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design and scope of the study.

claim: More than 70 genes demonstrated essential structural, functional, and developmental roles in the Drosophila heart.
source: Quantitative analyses of multiple cardiac phenotypes demonstrated essential structural, functional, and developmental roles for more than 70 genes, including a subgroup encoding histone H3K4 modifying proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative analyses performed in the study.

claim: A subgroup of the tested genes encode histone H3K4 modifying proteins.
source: Quantitative analyses of multiple cardiac phenotypes demonstrated essential structural, functional, and developmental roles for more than 70 genes, including a subgroup encoding histone H3K4 modifying proteins.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in the results.

claim: Drosophila can be used to evaluate cardiac phenotypes resulting from specific, patient-derived alleles of candidate disease genes.
source: We also demonstrated the use of Drosophila to evaluate cardiac phenotypes resulting from specific, patient-derived alleles of candidate disease genes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the gene replacement experiments with WDR5 alleles.

claim: 75% of human disease associated genes are represented in the fly genome by functional homologs.
source: It has been established that 75% of human disease associated genes are represented in the fly genome by functional homologs (Reiter et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Congenital heart disease affects 0.8% of live births.
source: Congenital heart disease (CHD) affects 0.8% of live births (Hoffman, 1990, 2002; Reller et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: Genetic factors are strongly implicated in CHD pathogenesis.
source: Genetic factors are strongly implicated in CHD pathogenesis, but the great majority of genes (accounting for an estimated 75% of cases) remain unidentified (Gelb et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The great majority of CHD genes (accounting for an estimated 75% of cases) remain unidentified.
source: Genetic factors are strongly implicated in CHD pathogenesis, but the great majority of genes (accounting for an estimated 75% of cases) remain unidentified (Gelb et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The Drosophila heart is a rhythmically beating linear tube composed of parallel rows of fused contractile cardiac cells, flanked by adherent pericardial cells.
source: The Drosophila heart (Figure 1A) is a rhythmically beating linear tube composed of parallel rows of fused contractile cardiac cells, flanked by adherent pericardial cells (Vogler and Bodmer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by both citation and visual evidence in Figure 1A.

claim: The Drosophila heart functions to maintain circulation of hemolymph throughout the body cavity.
source: The heart functions to maintain circulation of hemolymph (insect 'blood') throughout the body cavity.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Drosophila heart function.

claim: In a typical beating cycle, hemolymph enters the posteriorly-located heart chamber in the abdomen and is pumped anteriorly through the aorta towards the head and brain.
source: In a typical beating cycle, hemolymph enters the posteriorly-located heart chamber in the abdomen and is pumped anteriorly through the aorta towards the head and brain.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Drosophila heart function.

claim: Drosophila and human heart development are both largely directed by the same highly conserved regulatory networks.
source: Although structurally of relatively low complexity, Drosophila and human heart development are both largely directed by the same highly conserved regulatory networks (Vogler and Bodmer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: 4XHand-Gal4 promotes significantly greater Gal4 mRNA production than the single Hand enhancer.
source: The 4XHand enhancer promotes significantly greater Gal4 mRNA production than the single Hand enhancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 4XHand induced significantly greater knockdown of CG8184 mRNA when driving expression of the CG8184-IR RNAi silencing transgene compared to the single Hand enhancer.
source: Compared to the single Hand enhancer, 4XHand induced significantly greater knockdown of CG8184 (the homolog of human HUWE1) mRNA when driving expression of the CG8184-IR RNAi silencing transgene.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 4XHand induced significantly greater knockdown of Lid mRNA when driving expression of the Lid-IR RNAi silencing transgene compared to the single Hand enhancer.
source: Compared to the single Hand enhancer, 4XHand induced significantly greater knockdown of Lid (the homolog of human KDM5A and KDM5B) mRNA when driving expression of the Lid-IR RNAi silencing transgene.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Significant developmental lethal effects of heart-specific gene silencing were only observed in progeny flies carrying the 4XHand-Gal4 driver.
source: Significant developmental lethal effects of heart-specific gene silencing were only observed in progeny flies carrying the 4XHand-Gal4 driver.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mortality index data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PCGC study published 249 protein-altering de novo mutations from 362 severe cases of CHD.
source: The initial report (Zaidi et al., 2013) of 249 protein-altering de novo mutations from 362 severe cases of CHD identified 223 candidate disease genes involved in diverse biochemical pathways, with 26 genes selected as particular genes-of-interest based upon bioinformatics criteria (Zaidi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the PCGC study.

claim: The PCGC study identified 223 candidate disease genes involved in diverse biochemical pathways.
source: The initial report (Zaidi et al., 2013) of 249 protein-altering de novo mutations from 362 severe cases of CHD identified 223 candidate disease genes involved in diverse biochemical pathways, with 26 genes selected as particular genes-of-interest based upon bioinformatics criteria (Zaidi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the PCGC study.

claim: 26 genes were selected as particular genes-of-interest based upon bioinformatics criteria in the PCGC study.
source: The initial report (Zaidi et al., 2013) of 249 protein-altering de novo mutations from 362 severe cases of CHD identified 223 candidate disease genes involved in diverse biochemical pathways, with 26 genes selected as particular genes-of-interest based upon bioinformatics criteria (Zaidi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the PCGC study.

claim: 174 genes (78%) from the PCGC study had clear fly homologs.
source: 174 genes (78%) had clear fly homologs, consistent with the published estimate of 75% conservation of disease gene homologs (Reiter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis performed on the PCGC gene list.

claim: All of the 'top 26' genes identified by the PCGC study have conserved Drosophila homologs.
source: Interestingly, the 'top 26' genes identified by the PCGC study (Zaidi et al., 2013) all have conserved Drosophila homologs.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis performed on the top 26 genes.

claim: 52% of the tested fly homologs are required for cardiac development and function in flies.
source: We found that 52% of the tested fly homologs are required for cardiac development and function in flies.
evidence: This is a summary of the screening results from the study.

claim: The distribution of MI values across all ranges was not significantly different for the top 26 genes compared to the entire cohort of 134 candidate genes tested.
source: Importantly, we found that the distribution of MI values across all ranges was not significantly different for the top 26 genes compared to the entire cohort of 134 candidate genes tested (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparative analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Selection of candidate CHD genes on the basis of bioinformatics criteria alone did not enrich for genes inducing more severe developmental mortality phenotypes.
source: Thus, selection of candidate CHD genes on the basis of bioinformatics criteria alone did not enrich for genes inducing more severe developmental mortality phenotypes (indicative of more genes with essential roles in either heart development, tissue maintenance, or function).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MI distribution data comparing top 26 genes to all 134 genes.

claim: Only 6% of approximately 800 randomly chosen Drosophila genes showed any level of developmental lethality when silenced using the 4XHand-Gal4; UAS-RNAi system.
source: We found that only 6% of these genes showed any level of developmental lethality when silenced (i.e. 94% normal).
evidence: This claim is based on data from a previous screen of unbiased genes.

claim: The PCGC genomic association study enriched significantly for heart-essential genes as assayed in Drosophila.
source: Thus, the PCGC genomic association study, though not gene selection based upon bioinformatics criteria, did enrich significantly for heart-essential genes as assayed in Drosophila.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the PCGC gene set to unbiased genes.

claim: High heart expression (HHE) during development did not correlate with greater severity of developmental lethality associated with gene silencing in Drosophila heart.
source: As shown in Figure 2C, high heart expression (HHE) during development did not correlate with greater severity of developmental lethality associated with gene silencing in Drosophila heart.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Low heart expression (LHE) of murine homologs was associated with relatively higher severity of Drosophila gene silencing.
source: Contrary to expectation, low heart expression (LHE) of murine homologs was associated with relatively higher severity of Drosophila gene silencing.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Phylogenetic conservation correlated positively with Mortality Index.
source: When mortality was assayed as a function of degree of fly-human conservation among all 134 tested genes (Figure 2D) we did observe greater mortality among highly conserved genes compared to less conserved genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Heart RNA levels of six tested target genes were all significantly reduced by RNAi silencing.
source: As shown in Figure 3, heart RNA levels of target genes were all significantly reduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Consistent MI results were obtained for all top 26 genes using two or more independent RNAi silencing fly lines for each gene.
source: Furthermore, we tested developmental lethal phenotypes for all top 26 genes using two or more independent RNAi silencing fly lines for each gene, and obtained consistent MI results in all cases (data not shown).
evidence: This is a statement about the reproducibility of the results.

claim: Eight of the top 26 gene homologs encode products involved in histone H3K4 and H3K27 methylation.
source: Eight of the top 26 gene homologs encode products involved in histone H3K4 and H3K27 methylation (Figures 2A and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in Figures 2A and 4.

claim: Epigenetic activating (H3K4me) and inactivating (H3K27me) marks are associated with selective activation of promoters and enhancers.
source: Epigenetic activating (H3K4me) and inactivating (H3K27me) marks are associated with selective activation of promoters and enhancers, and chromatin marks are associated with specification and differentiation of cardiac cells (Wamstad et al., 2012), murine heart development (He et al., 2012; Delgado-Olguín et al., 2012), and cardiac pathogenesis (Kaneda et al., 2009; Zhang and Liu, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Chromatin marks are associated with specification and differentiation of cardiac cells.
source: Epigenetic activating (H3K4me) and inactivating (H3K27me) marks are associated with selective activation of promoters and enhancers, and chromatin marks are associated with specification and differentiation of cardiac cells (Wamstad et al., 2012), murine heart development (He et al., 2012; Delgado-Olguín et al., 2012), and cardiac pathogenesis (Kaneda et al., 2009; Zhang and Liu, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Chromatin marks are associated with murine heart development.
source: Epigenetic activating (H3K4me) and inactivating (H3K27me) marks are associated with selective activation of promoters and enhancers, and chromatin marks are associated with specification and differentiation of cardiac cells (Wamstad et al., 2012), murine heart development (He et al., 2012; Delgado-Olguín et al., 2012), and cardiac pathogenesis (Kaneda et al., 2009; Zhang and Liu, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Chromatin marks are associated with cardiac pathogenesis.
source: Epigenetic activating (H3K4me) and inactivating (H3K27me) marks are associated with selective activation of promoters and enhancers, and chromatin marks are associated with specification and differentiation of cardiac cells (Wamstad et al., 2012), murine heart development (He et al., 2012; Delgado-Olguín et al., 2012), and cardiac pathogenesis (Kaneda et al., 2009; Zhang and Liu, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: 42% of the top candidate genes from the PCGC study are involved in histone modification pathways.
source: Thus 42% of the top candidate genes from the PCGC study are involved in histone modification pathways, and all but one are highly conserved.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the data presented about the top 26 genes.

claim: All but one of the histone modification pathway genes among the top 26 are highly conserved.
source: Thus 42% of the top candidate genes from the PCGC study are involved in histone modification pathways, and all but one are highly conserved.
evidence: This is a statement based on the conservation analysis of the top 26 genes.

claim: Silencing kismet yielded an adult heart phenotype in which the heart tube was severely affected with very low cardiac myofibrillar density.
source: Silencing kismet yielded an adult heart phenotype in which the heart tube was severely affected (Figure 4B) with very low cardiac myofibrillar density (Figure 4C), elevated Pericardin (collagen) deposition (Figure 4D), and reduced numbers of cardioblasts (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4B-E.

claim: Silencing kismet resulted in elevated Pericardin (collagen) deposition.
source: Silencing kismet yielded an adult heart phenotype in which the heart tube was severely affected (Figure 4B) with very low cardiac myofibrillar density (Figure 4C), elevated Pericardin (collagen) deposition (Figure 4D), and reduced numbers of cardioblasts (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Silencing kismet resulted in reduced numbers of cardioblasts.
source: Silencing kismet yielded an adult heart phenotype in which the heart tube was severely affected (Figure 4B) with very low cardiac myofibrillar density (Figure 4C), elevated Pericardin (collagen) deposition (Figure 4D), and reduced numbers of cardioblasts (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Adult fly longevity was significantly affected by kismet silencing, with approximately 50% of flies dead by day 25.
source: Adult fly longevity was significantly affected, with approximately 50% of flies dead by day 25 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the survival data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: During development, kismet silencing caused 54% mortality.
source: During development, kismet silencing caused 54% mortality (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mortality index data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In larvae, cardiac myofibrillar density was reduced with pronounced heart tube filament disruption upon kismet silencing.
source: In larvae, cardiac myofibrillar density was reduced with pronounced heart tube filament disruption (Figure 4G,H), and Pericardin over-expression with disorganized ECM deposition (Figure 4G,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4G and 4H.

claim: Kismet silencing resulted in Pericardin over-expression with disorganized ECM deposition in larvae.
source: In larvae, cardiac myofibrillar density was reduced with pronounced heart tube filament disruption (Figure 4G,H), and Pericardin over-expression with disorganized ECM deposition (Figure 4G,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4G and 4I.

claim: Trx-silenced adult flies lacked cardiac actin and heart tube.
source: Trx-silenced adult flies lacked cardiac actin and heart tube (Figure 4B,C), exhibited severely reduced Pericardin (Figure 4D), almost no cardioblast cells (Figure 4E), and all were dead at day 25 after emergence, compared to 20% mortality among control flies (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: Trx-silenced adult flies exhibited severely reduced Pericardin.
source: Trx-silenced adult flies lacked cardiac actin and heart tube (Figure 4B,C), exhibited severely reduced Pericardin (Figure 4D), almost no cardioblast cells (Figure 4E), and all were dead at day 25 after emergence, compared to 20% mortality among control flies (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Trx-silenced adult flies had almost no cardioblast cells.
source: Trx-silenced adult flies lacked cardiac actin and heart tube (Figure 4B,C), exhibited severely reduced Pericardin (Figure 4D), almost no cardioblast cells (Figure 4E), and all were dead at day 25 after emergence, compared to 20% mortality among control flies (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: All Trx-silenced flies were dead at day 25 after emergence, compared to 20% mortality among control flies.
source: Trx-silenced adult flies lacked cardiac actin and heart tube (Figure 4B,C), exhibited severely reduced Pericardin (Figure 4D), almost no cardioblast cells (Figure 4E), and all were dead at day 25 after emergence, compared to 20% mortality among control flies (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the survival data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Trx silencing caused 35% developmental lethality.
source: Trx silencing caused 35% developmental lethality (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mortality index data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In larvae, knock down of trx induced abnormal heart tube structure with reduced cardiac myofibrillar density and reduced Pericardin.
source: In larvae, knock down of trx induced abnormal heart tube structure (Figure 4G) with reduced cardiac myofibrillar density (Figure 4G,H) and reduced Pericardin (Figure 4G,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4G, 4H, and 4I.

claim: Silencing of wds caused complete developmental lethality.
source: Silencing of wds caused complete developmental lethality (Figure 2A) and a dramatic larva heart phenotype (Figure 4G) featuring abnormal cardiac actin organization and fiber density (Figure 4H), and extremely high levels of Pericardin (Figure 4G,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mortality index data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Silencing of wds resulted in a dramatic larva heart phenotype featuring abnormal cardiac actin organization and fiber density, and extremely high levels of Pericardin.
source: Silencing of wds caused complete developmental lethality (Figure 2A) and a dramatic larva heart phenotype (Figure 4G) featuring abnormal cardiac actin organization and fiber density (Figure 4H), and extremely high levels of Pericardin (Figure 4G,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4G, 4H, and 4I.

claim: H3K4 methylation is critical for normal heart development and function.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that H3K4 methylation is critical for normal heart development and function, a conclusion supported by the observation that knockdown of the H3K4 de-methylase Lid had no phenotypic consequences (Figure 4C–F,H,I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results of silencing H3K4 methylation pathway genes.

claim: Knockdown of the H3K4 de-methylase Lid had no phenotypic consequences.
source: Taken together, these results strongly suggest that H3K4 methylation is critical for normal heart development and function, a conclusion supported by the observation that knockdown of the H3K4 de-methylase Lid had no phenotypic consequences (Figure 4C–F,H,I; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4C-F, 4H, 4I, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Silencing of SMOX resulted in minimal developmental mortality (MI 7%).
source: Similarly, silencing of SMOX (involved in H3K27 de-methylation) resulted in minimal developmental mortality (MI 7%, Figure 2A) but normal cardiac myofibrillar density and Pericardin levels in larvae (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mortality index data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Silencing of SMOX resulted in normal cardiac myofibrillar density and Pericardin levels in larvae.
source: Similarly, silencing of SMOX (involved in H3K27 de-methylation) resulted in minimal developmental mortality (MI 7%, Figure 2A) but normal cardiac myofibrillar density and Pericardin levels in larvae (Figure 4H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4H and 4I.

claim: The adult heart phenotype of SMOX silencing was essentially normal, as was adult mortality at day 25.
source: The adult heart phenotype was essentially normal, as was adult mortality at day 25 (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Ubiquitination of H2BK120 is required for H3K4 methylation.
source: Ubiquitination of H2BK120 (Figure 4A) is required for H3K4 methylation, and we observed that silencing of the UbcD6 gene resulted in 84% developmental mortality (Figure 2A) and reduced adult longevity (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about histone modification.

claim: Silencing of the UbcD6 gene resulted in 84% developmental mortality.
source: Ubiquitination of H2BK120 (Figure 4A) is required for H3K4 methylation, and we observed that silencing of the UbcD6 gene resulted in 84% developmental mortality (Figure 2A) and reduced adult longevity (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mortality index data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Silencing of UbcD6 resulted in reduced adult longevity.
source: Ubiquitination of H2BK120 (Figure 4A) is required for H3K4 methylation, and we observed that silencing of the UbcD6 gene resulted in 84% developmental mortality (Figure 2A) and reduced adult longevity (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the survival data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The adult heart of UbcD6-silenced flies was severely affected with greatly reduced cardiac myofibrillar density, elevated Pericardin, and reduced cardioblast cell numbers.
source: The adult heart was severely affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) with greatly reduced cardiac myofibrillar density (Figure 4C), elevated Pericardin (Figure 4D), and reduced cardioblast cell numbers (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4C, 4D, 4E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Silencing of Bre1 and Scny caused developmental mortality.
source: Silencing of Bre1 and Scny also caused developmental mortality and cardiac myofibrillar density was somewhat reduced in larvae and adults (Figure 4C,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mortality index data and the data shown in Figures 4C and 4H.

claim: Cardiac myofibrillar density was somewhat reduced in larvae and adults upon silencing of Bre1 and Scny.
source: Silencing of Bre1 and Scny also caused developmental mortality and cardiac myofibrillar density was somewhat reduced in larvae and adults (Figure 4C,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4C and 4H.

claim: Pericardin levels, cardioblast cell numbers, and adult mortality at day 25 were essentially normal upon silencing of Bre1 and Scny.
source: Pericardin levels, cardioblast cell numbers, and adult mortality at day 25 were essentially normal (Figure 4D,E,F,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 4D, 4E, 4F, and 4I.

claim: H3K4 de-methylation did not appear critical as evidenced by the essentially normal heart phenotype, normal MI, and normal adult longevity observed upon Lid silencing.
source: By contrast, H3K4 de-methylation did not appear critical as evidenced by the essentially normal heart phenotype, normal MI, and normal adult longevity observed upon Lid silencing. (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results of Lid silencing experiments.

claim: In normal control flies fluorescent dye is readily detectable in the head within 15 s of injection, and significantly accumulated by 30 s.
source: We observed that in normal control flies fluorescent dye is readily detectable in the head within 15 s of injection, and significantly accumulated by 30 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dye angiography data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Silencing of candidate CHD gene homologs involved in the methylation of H3K4 and H3K27 profoundly impaired cardiac function.
source: By contrast, silencing of candidate CHD gene homologs involved in the methylation of H3K4 and H3K27 profoundly impaired cardiac function (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the dye angiography data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Silencing of Smox and Lid did not measurably impair heart function as measured by dye angiography.
source: Silencing of Smox and Lid, however, did not measurably impair heart function as measured in this assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dye angiography data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: H3K4 and H3K27 methylation, and not demethylation, is essential for heart function.
source: These observations indicate that H3K4 and H3K27 methylation, and not demethylation, is essential for heart function, consistent with our findings with regard to cardiac tissue morphology and effects on developmental lethality and adult longevity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined results of the functional assays.

claim: Heart-specific silencing of wds caused 100% developmental lethality.
source: Heart-specific silencing of wds caused 100% developmental lethality and abnormal heart morphology in late larvae characterized by reduced cardiac myofibers and severe over-deposition of Pericardin (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Heart-specific silencing of wds resulted in abnormal heart morphology in late larvae characterized by reduced cardiac myofibers and severe over-deposition of Pericardin.
source: Heart-specific silencing of wds caused 100% developmental lethality and abnormal heart morphology in late larvae characterized by reduced cardiac myofibers and severe over-deposition of Pericardin (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figures 6B, 6C, and 6D.

claim: Simultaneously overexpressing a wild type human WDR5 allele reduced developmental lethality almost 7-fold.
source: We found that simultaneously overexpressing a wild type human WDR5 allele reduced developmental lethality almost 7-fold, significantly restored cardiac myofibrillar density, and reduced Pericardin levels essentially to normal (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpressing wild type human WDR5 significantly restored cardiac myofibrillar density.
source: We found that simultaneously overexpressing a wild type human WDR5 allele reduced developmental lethality almost 7-fold, significantly restored cardiac myofibrillar density, and reduced Pericardin levels essentially to normal (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Overexpressing wild type human WDR5 reduced Pericardin levels essentially to normal.
source: We found that simultaneously overexpressing a wild type human WDR5 allele reduced developmental lethality almost 7-fold, significantly restored cardiac myofibrillar density, and reduced Pericardin levels essentially to normal (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: When the endogenous wds expression was 'replaced' by a CHD patient-derived WDR5-K7Q mutant allele, developmental lethality remained quite elevated.
source: By contrast, when the endogenous wds expression was 'replaced' by a CHD patient-derived WDR5-K7Q mutant allele, developmental lethality remained quite elevated, cardiac myofibrillar density remained abnormally low (relative both to Control and wild type WDR5 rescue), and Pericardin levels were lowered but still significantly higher than both Control and wild type WDR5 rescue.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: When the endogenous wds expression was 'replaced' by a CHD patient-derived WDR5-K7Q mutant allele, cardiac myofibrillar density remained abnormally low (relative both to Control and wild type WDR5 rescue).
source: By contrast, when the endogenous wds expression was 'replaced' by a CHD patient-derived WDR5-K7Q mutant allele, developmental lethality remained quite elevated, cardiac myofibrillar density remained abnormally low (relative both to Control and wild type WDR5 rescue), and Pericardin levels were lowered but still significantly higher than both Control and wild type WDR5 rescue.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When the endogenous wds expression was 'replaced' by a CHD patient-derived WDR5-K7Q mutant allele, Pericardin levels were lowered but still significantly higher than both Control and wild type WDR5 rescue.
source: By contrast, when the endogenous wds expression was 'replaced' by a CHD patient-derived WDR5-K7Q mutant allele, developmental lethality remained quite elevated, cardiac myofibrillar density remained abnormally low (relative both to Control and wild type WDR5 rescue), and Pericardin levels were lowered but still significantly higher than both Control and wild type WDR5 rescue.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Approximately 25% of human disease genes are not represented by Drosophila homologs.
source: From the outset, of human disease genes, approximately 25% are not represented by Drosophila homologs.
evidence: This is based on the established knowledge that 75% of human disease genes have Drosophila homologs.

claim: The in vivo screening system rapidly and efficiently confirmed roles in heart development, tissue maintenance, or cardiac function for 72 candidate genes.
source: Nevertheless, our in vivo screening system rapidly and efficiently confirmed roles in heart development, tissue maintenance, or cardiac function for 72 candidate genes.
evidence: This is a summary of the screening results from the study.

claim: Drosophila has served as a model to study genes related to CHD for over 20 years.
source: Drosophila has served as a model to study genes related to CHD for over 20 years, based on the evolutionarily conserved genetic basis of heart development (Bier and Bodmer, 2004; Olson, 2006; Yi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The use of Drosophila as a CHD model is based on the evolutionarily conserved genetic basis of heart development.
source: Drosophila has served as a model to study genes related to CHD for over 20 years, based on the evolutionarily conserved genetic basis of heart development (Bier and Bodmer, 2004; Olson, 2006; Yi et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Use of Drosophila as a model to elucidate molecular disease mechanisms is well established and amply documented.
source: Use of Drosophila as a model to elucidate molecular disease mechanisms is well established and amply documented (Cagan, 2011; Na et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2013; Diop and Bodmer, 2015; Bier and Bodmer, 2004; Owusu-Ansah and Perrimon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: A definitive assignment of disease association should be established through the analysis of mutant gene phenotypes in a mammalian model.
source: While a definitive assignment of disease association should be established through the analysis of mutant gene phenotypes in a mammalian model, this approach is not practical for rapid high-throughput initial screening of large numbers of candidate genes.
evidence: This is a statement about the gold standard for disease gene validation.

claim: Analysis of mutant gene phenotypes in a mammalian model is not practical for rapid high-throughput initial screening of large numbers of candidate genes.
source: While a definitive assignment of disease association should be established through the analysis of mutant gene phenotypes in a mammalian model, this approach is not practical for rapid high-throughput initial screening of large numbers of candidate genes.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of mammalian models for high-throughput screening.

claim: Drosophila possesses the attributes of a simple animal model system that make it ideally suited for rapid high-throughput initial screening.
source: Drosophila, by contrast, possesses the attributes of a simple animal model system that make it ideally suited for this role (Bier, 2005; Chien et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Hand enhancer is active during development from embryonic stages.
source: The Hand enhancer is active during development from embryonic stages, and we reasoned that Hand enhancer-driven silencing of genes known to be essential for heart development would cause developmental lethality.
evidence: This is a statement about the temporal expression pattern of the Hand enhancer.

claim: Hand enhancer-driven silencing of genes known to be essential for heart development would cause developmental lethality.
